extracted.intended_audience: ProofWiki contributors and editors (active page authors and seasoned editors)
extracted.subtask_description: House-style and source/coding conventions for writing and editing mathematical proof and definition pages on ProofWiki, covering linking, LaTeX, notation, linguistic style, sources, and page-structure practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: References to Theorems and Axioms
rubrics_metrics.description: Whenever a theorem is invoked or referred to, it should be referenced by its full title. Use the page title (double-square-bracket link) and do not change case; for axioms use the provided template.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: "By Union Distributes over Intersection, A ∪ (B ∩ C) = (A ∪ B) ∩ (A ∪ C)." Implement as [[Union Distributes over Intersection]]. For axioms use the Axiom-link template: {{Axiom-link|Choice}} producing 'Axiom of Choice'.

rubrics_metrics.name: References to Definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Whenever a concept (or part of it) is invoked, present it as a link to the definition page; it is preferred that every use of the word be linked.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use non-intrusive linking: write 'Let R be a ring.' linking 'ring' to Definition:Ring rather than embedding the full page title. Prefer linking each occurrence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permanent Redirects to Definitions on Subpages
rubrics_metrics.description: If a definition lives on a subpage, use (or create) a permanent redirect to that subpage and link to the redirect instead of directly linking the subpage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'What links here' to find existing redirects; if none exist, create one. Exception: when subpages handle multiple distinct definitions (Definition:Prime Number/Definition 1, etc.), do not invoke the individual subpage unless necessary (e.g., to avoid circularity or when proving equivalence).

rubrics_metrics.name: Symbol Set
rubrics_metrics.description: Only standard alphanumeric and punctuation characters from a standard English keyboard are accepted in ProofWiki LaTeX source; letters with diacritics should not be used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use LaTeX commands for non-English characters and mathematical symbols (e.g., use \alpha for α). Exceptions: reporting mathematician names with diacritics and linguistic derivations (language notes) where direct characters may be used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inline Equations
rubrics_metrics.description: Inline equations should be delimited by dollar signs ($...$).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: The semilinear wave equation $\partial_t U = A U + \map B U$ is Hamiltonian — produced by inserting $...$ in the sentence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Displayed Equations (indentation vs centering)
rubrics_metrics.description: Displayed equations should be indented using a single colon rather than centered with $$ to preserve short-sentence flow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use ":$...$" for displayed equations (and the \ds convenience macro). Avoid using $$E = m c^2$$ centered display because it breaks reading flow with short sentences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use \ds for Big Operators
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the \ds command at the front of expressions using big operators (\sum, \prod, \frac, \binom, \lim, \int, \bigcup, \bigcap, etc.) whether inline or displayed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: \ds \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n, \ds \frac{-b \pm \sqrt{b^2-4ac}}{2a}. When characters like '=' or '\in' appear in subscripts of big operators, use \mathop to enforce spacing: \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abbreviated Big Symbols (\dfrac, \dbinom)
rubrics_metrics.description: Allow use of \dfrac and \dbinom as abbreviated big versions (d = display); they can be used inside \ds expressions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preference for consistency: feel free to use \dfrac and \dbinom throughout; if other big operators are present, \ds is still required.

rubrics_metrics.name: The d of Calculus
rubrics_metrics.description: Typeset the differential 'd' in non-italic form using \d or \rd (\rd includes a half-space for integrals).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write \dfrac{\d y}{\d x} not \dfrac{d y}{d x}. Use \rd for integrals: \int f(x) \rd x.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fonts and Which to Use
rubrics_metrics.description: Several math fonts are available with conventional uses (\mathcal, \mathbb or \Bbb, \mathscr, \mathsf, \mathfrak, \mathtt). Fraktur and Script are discouraged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use \T and \F macros for True/False, and provided shortcuts for \N, \Z, \Q, \R, \C and \GF. Note site-specific shortcuts like \AA, \BB for \mathcal letters. Prefer fonts that are readable across browsers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Logical Symbols in Mathematical Exposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Reserve logical notation (\land, \lor) for logic; prefer writing out 'and' and 'or' in general mathematical exposition to avoid ambiguity with field-specific meanings (meet/join).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write '...: λ_y = y * I_R and ρ_y = I_R * y' instead of using \land unless the context is logic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punctuation for Sentences Broken by Displayed Equations
rubrics_metrics.description: A sentence that is broken by a displayed equation should be ended with a colon; the displayed equation itself should not be ended with a full stop or comma inside the LaTeX.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write: 'Let: \ds ... where ...' and do not place punctuation inside the displayed math (avoid producing '... }.$' inside math). Commas should be used only for list separation, not to join clauses in proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Q.E.D. / Proof Terminator
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the {{qed}} template to end proofs (produces \blacksquare); for subproofs use {{qed|lemma}} (produces \Box).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place the template immediately after the last line of the proof: 'Hence the result. {{qed}}' — do not put a blank line before the template. Do not write 'Q.E.D.' as text.

rubrics_metrics.name: LaTeX Source Spacing Conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Backslash commands and each variable should be preceded by a space in source (except when enclosing things in brackets); insert spaces between adjacent curly braces to avoid interpreter issues in templates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples show consistent spacing. When writing \paren{...}, use \paren { ... } in source style where appropriate to improve readability of source code.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use \paren for Brackets; avoid manual \big commands
rubrics_metrics.description: When enclosing brackets, use the \paren{...} command rather than literal parentheses or ad-hoc size commands (\big, \Big, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: \paren auto-sizes parentheses aesthetically; avoid \big, \Big, etc. which are usually unnecessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punctuation Outside Math Environments
rubrics_metrics.description: If punctuation is necessary, place it outside the LaTeX environment rather than inside.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write 'Hence $\map f {\sin x}$.' with the period outside the math code; avoid 'Hence $\map f {\sin x}.$' which places punctuation inside the math environment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single-Character Parameters Need Not Use Braces
rubrics_metrics.description: Single-character parameters to standard LaTeX constructs may omit curly braces for readability (e.g., \dfrac 1 2 preferred to \dfrac {1} {2}).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both forms render the same, but \dfrac12 is harder to read; prefer spacing like \dfrac 1 2 for clarity while respecting spacing rules elsewhere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aligned Material / eqn Template Usage
rubrics_metrics.description: If an equation includes multiple equalities/inequalities, place each equality on a new line using the {{eqn}} template (or equivalent). The eqn environment is already in \displaystyle mode.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure: {{begin-eqn}} {{eqn | l = ... | r = ... }} ... {{end-eqn}}. Omit empty columns, align '|' and '=' characters in source, use | c = for comments (not LaTeX), and avoid two consecutive curly braces '{{' or '}}' inside eqn. Do not use the pipe '|' inside LaTeX — use \vert or \lvert/\rvert and \Vert for double vertical bars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid Breaking eqn Interpreter (braces/pipes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Within {{eqn}} do not include two consecutive curly braces '{{' or '}}' and avoid pipe characters '|' in LaTeX expressions; use \vert/\lvert/\rvert and \Vert instead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If copying LaTeX into eqn templates, replace '|' with \vert or appropriate macros and put spaces between curly braces where needed to prevent template parse errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language of Pages
rubrics_metrics.description: All pages are to be presented in English; where US vs other spellings differ, US English is generally used (with a few exceptions under discussion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be consistent with US spellings unless there is a documented exception (e.g., metre in active discussion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal Linguistic Style
rubrics_metrics.description: During mathematical exposition, prefer a formal style; avoid colloquial language except for illustrative examples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'Suppose that ...' rather than 'Let's suppose that ...'; prefer 'Hence the result.' over '... and we're done.' Maintain formal tone to appeal to a wide, international audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of 'Let' vs 'Suppose'
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Let' should introduce the existence of an entity; 'Suppose' should introduce an entity whose existence is in question (e.g., in proof by contradiction).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Let S be a set.' vs 'Suppose T ⊆ S such that |T| > |S|.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid Ambiguous 'Any'
rubrics_metrics.description: The word 'any' can be ambiguous and is discouraged; prefer 'every' or 'an arbitrary' where appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Replace 'any' with clearer quantification: 'every element' or 'an arbitrary element' to avoid ambiguity between existential and universal readings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abbreviations (e.g., e.g., i.e.) and Contractions
rubrics_metrics.description: Discourage use of Latin abbreviations 'e.g.' and 'i.e.' due to common misuse; avoid contractions like "it's" — use 'it is'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer writing out 'for example' and 'that is' or other clear phrasing. Ensure 'its' vs 'it's' is used correctly; prefer 'it is' over 'it's' to avoid contractions in formal exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sentence Length and Short-Sentence House Style
rubrics_metrics.description: Each sentence should be short and convey one step (one simple statement or one compound 'P, therefore Q'); each sentence should be on a separate line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid long nested sentences; break proofs into short numbered/line-separated steps. Anti-pattern examples shown (long tangled single-paragraph proofs) — do not imitate those.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid Parenthetical Notes in-line
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid inserting parenthetical material inside sentences; parenthetical notes often conflict with short-sentence style and can confuse notation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If extra information is necessary, provide it in a separate sentence or a clarifying line; avoid constructs like 'f_n(x) ∈ Σ (where f_n(x) is a family ...)' inside a single sentence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimize Filler Words; Prefer Terse Clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Use as terse a form as possible; remove unnecessary filler words (e.g., 'it follows that', 'we have') unless they aid clarity or completeness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When citing results, prefer 'From Fred's Theorem, Q.' rather than 'We have that ...'. Clarity overrides terseness when needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions: Use 'is' Form
rubrics_metrics.description: In definitions, use simple 'X is Y' phrasing rather than verbose constructs like 'X is called', 'X is known as', etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer 'X is a group' rather than 'X is called a group' or 'X is said to be a group'. Keep definitions concise and direct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid Empty Statements and Waffle
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not include statements that impart no information (e.g., 'The first part of the proof is easy', 'This article is complete as far as it goes...').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use templates like {{handwaving}}, {{explain}}, or {{Proofread}} where appropriate; avoid filler commentary and incomplete placeholder text. Remove or replace boilerplate that does not add content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalization after Displayed Equations
rubrics_metrics.description: When a sentence is continued after a displayed equation (or when a 'where' clause continues the sentence), do not begin the continuation with a capital letter — it is not a new sentence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep continuation words lowercase: after 'Let: \ds S = ...' continue 'where \ds \sum denotes summation.' Avoid capitalizing 'Where' in continuations unless it truly starts a new sentence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sources: Ordering and Citation Granularity
rubrics_metrics.description: List multiple sources in chronological order, then alphabetically by the first author's surname. When referencing specific entries, always use chapter/section/entry identifiers rather than page numbers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide chapter and section titles when possible. Use the bulleted list format recommended by Help:Page Editing. Page numbers are discouraged because pagination varies across editions and reprints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of Sources and Templates
rubrics_metrics.description: Use provided templates for different source types (Template:BookReference for books, Template:Citation for journal articles, and various online source templates: MathWorld, PlanetMath, MacTutor, KhanAcademy, Metamath, Mizar, OEIS, SpringerOnline, Stackexchange).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples given for each template use. Ensure you cite the specific work entry (chapter/section) rather than a page number. Use StackExchange links only to answers and only in specified circumstances (OP tried hard; or result only documented on SE).

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptability of Online Sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Only certain online resources (the listed templates and scholarly papers available online) are acceptable; some online materials are not acceptable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not generally acceptable: university lecture notes (unstable), homework-help forums, discussion pages on any web forum, and Wikipedia (prefer primary sources). Scholarly papers available online are usually okay. The listed templates (MathWorld, PlanetMath, etc.) are currently the only web resources to be used as general citation sources unless explicitly extended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Splitting Sources Across Multiple Pages
rubrics_metrics.description: If a source (theorem, proof, definition) is split across multiple pages, reference the source on every page and update the process flow according to the order elements appear in the source.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When splitting content, ensure each resulting page contains the appropriate citation and the sequence of source elements follows the original source ordering for clarity and maintenance.
